# Effective is not enough: Pérez López's freely-adaptive system and the two kinds of learning an autonomous system needs

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that an autonomous system is under control when every action it takes is scored on whether it reached its own target. This paper argues otherwise: an action can reach its target and still push something else the system needs out of its limits. A system has to score both, learn which of its actions keep doing harm, and drop them, or it learns only half of what experience teaches.

Pérez López took Ashby's ultrastable system from the organism to the organization. He shows that every action has to be judged twice, on whether it reached its goal and on what it did to everything else the system needs, and that an organization survives only while it is effective, attractive and consistent at once. We state each of his points as a property this system can fail, measure it from the system's own ledgers, and built the reading that was missing: a second verdict on every settled action and the three survival levels.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 7 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

Ashby's ultrastable system explains how an organism learns to keep its essential variables in limits, but nature builds that mechanism into organisms and no one builds it into organizations, so it must be built on purpose. Every action has an effectiveness (its explicit, predictable consequence), an efficiency (its consequences for the system's other needs, learned only by experience) and a consistency (how its efficiency changes as the system learns). An organization survives only if it is effective, attractive to its members and consistent at once. [1]

This matters now because the usual answer, hitting the target is enough, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. A control system that only corrects deviations from plans. In a stable system feedback only corrects deviations from a plan that someone outside set. In an ultrastable system the aim of the control function is twofold: "Ensure that plans are consistent with objectives" and "Ensure that plans are accomplished". A system whose work items carry no objective to be measured against can only do the second. [1]
2. Not knowing that an essential variable is disturbed. Nature has given organisms the mechanisms that keep essential variables in limits; it has not given them to organizations, so they must be built in on purpose. "An organism may die because it does not have a 'program' to cope with disturbances in the value of its essential variables. An organization may die because it does not know that its essential variables are disturbed." [1]
3. Scoring only whether an action reached its target. An action is effective when it reaches its explicit goal and efficient when its unsought consequences do not offset that. Barnard runs the two together, but they teach different things: when the predicted result does not happen, the model is incorrect; when it happens and produces offsetting dissatisfactions, the model is incomplete. A system that scores only predictions learns only the first. [1]
4. Repeating actions whose side effects keep growing. "An ultrastable system is one that has a built-in mechanism which ensures consistency, that is to say, a mechanism which systematically discards action alternatives that have been found to have decreasing efficiency after they were tried." [1]
5. Surviving on one level only. "An organization, to survive, must accomplish goals at all three levels": effective (it must generate more resources than are needed to motivate membership), attractive (it must create enough motivation in its members to persuade them to cooperate) and consistent (otherwise it lasts only as long as it can buy back lost attractiveness with greater rewards, until it needs more resources to motivate people than it obtains). [1]
6. A memory that leaves past mistakes out. Selective use of memory is central: an evoked set can leave out what shows that previous actions were wrong. The working paper defines "pride" as the attitude "which tends to eliminate from the 'evoked set' all those elements in memory which show that previous actions were wrong". A system that records its mistakes but lets nothing act on them has that blind spot. [1]
7. The member knowing better than the organization. Organizational values forbid tasks that do not satisfy a member's needs "even though that fact may not be known to the individual", and "an organization will be successful insofar as it knows better than the individual himself what actions by the individual will satisfy the individual's needs." Every owner intervention that corrects the system is a case where the reverse held. [1]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [2]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [3]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. A control system that only corrects deviations from plans: the system keeps its own goal hierarchy and turns bounded knobs toward each target (GOALS-1, `seed/worker/src/goals.js`); the goal furthest out of bounds becomes a task tree, gated on a fresh reading of that goal (PLAN-1, `seed/worker/src/planner.js`); a work item needs a done check, a prediction on a metric, an out-of-scope line and a live probe (SPEC-GATE-1, `seed/scripts/specgate.py`)
2. Not knowing that an essential variable is disturbed: every essential variable is read each tick; one that cannot be read is never in bounds and files its own UNMEASURED item (ULTRASTABILITY-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`); a reading with no data never counts as met (REDTEAM-1, `foundation/redteam.py`)
3. Scoring only whether an action reached its target: every settled decision, growth experiment and second-loop step gets an efficiency verdict beside its own: did another essential variable of its scope leave its limits while it was open (FREELY-ADAPTIVE-1, `foundation/freeadapt.py`); every decision logs its prediction and is scored against the measured outcome (the effectiveness verdict) (DECISIONS-1, `foundation/decisions.py`)
4. Repeating actions whose side effects keep growing: an action class whose recent actions mostly disturbed other essential variables files a Q-FAS item to redesign or retire it, closed only when the same reading passes (FREELY-ADAPTIVE-1, `foundation/freeadapt.py`); a second-loop step is kept only when its variable is back inside its limits; otherwise it is undone (ULTRASTABILITY-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)
5. Surviving on one level only: the three levels are read every pass: k at or above its floor, the share of the executor's attempts that are merged, and that share not falling between the earlier and later half (FREELY-ADAPTIVE-1, `foundation/freeadapt.py`); k = verified deploys over normalized cost and human touches, logged every tick (CRITICALITY-1, `foundation/criticality.py`); survival_levels is an essential variable held at 3, so the second loop acts when one level fails (ULTRASTABILITY-1, `doctrine/ultrastability.json`)
6. A memory that leaves past mistakes out: every recorded lesson is bound to a check, variable, detector or test, or carried by an open item until it is (LESSONS-1, `foundation/lessons.py`); every failure mode has a live detector and a failing one files its own item (FAILURE-RESOLVE-1, `foundation/failure_audit.py`)
7. The member knowing better than the organization: what the owner does not know is computed (known minus told), never asked (IGNORANCE-1, `foundation/ignorance.py`); a register of needs the owner is not expected to know, each with a probe (BLINDSPOT-1, `foundation/blindspots.py`); owner interventions are an essential variable held at 0 (SECOND-LOOP-2, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. A control system that only corrects deviations from plans. Put in place: the system keeps its own goal hierarchy and turns bounded knobs toward each target. Check it with one number, share of open work items with a done check, a prediction, an out-of-scope line and a live proof (foundation/specgate.py), and set a limit for it (>= 0.9 is the limit we use).
2. Not knowing that an essential variable is disturbed. Put in place: every essential variable is read each tick; one that cannot be read is never in bounds and files its own UNMEASURED item. Check it with one number, share of essential variables (platform and tenant) whose latest reading in the last 7 days has a value (ops/ultrastability.jsonl), and set a limit for it (>= 0.95 is the limit we use).
3. Scoring only whether an action reached its target. Put in place: every settled decision, growth experiment and second-loop step gets an efficiency verdict beside its own: did another essential variable of its scope leave its limits while it was open. Check it with one number, share of settled actions (decisions, growth experiments, second-loop steps) that carry an efficiency verdict as well as an effectiveness verdict (foundation/freeadapt.py), and set a limit for it (>= 0.8 is the limit we use).
4. Repeating actions whose side effects keep growing. Put in place: an action class whose recent actions mostly disturbed other essential variables files a Q-FAS item to redesign or retire it, closed only when the same reading passes. Check it with one number, share of judged action classes whose recent actions mostly left the other essential variables inside their limits (foundation/freeadapt.py), and set a limit for it (>= 0.9 is the limit we use).
5. Surviving on one level only. Put in place: the three levels are read every pass: k at or above its floor, the share of the executor's attempts that are merged, and that share not falling between the earlier and later half. Check it with one number, how many of the three survival levels hold now: effective, attractive, consistent (foundation/freeadapt.py), and set a limit for it (>= 3 is the limit we use).
6. A memory that leaves past mistakes out. Put in place: every recorded lesson is bound to a check, variable, detector or test, or carried by an open item until it is. Check it with one number, share of recorded lessons bound to a check, variable, detector or test (doctrine/lessons.json), and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
7. The member knowing better than the organization. Put in place: what the owner does not know is computed (known minus told), never asked. Check it with one number, owner-driven thread sessions that changed the repository in the last 7 days (ops/provenance.jsonl), and set a limit for it (<= 0 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 2 of 7 of these checks pass today. Share of open work items with a done check, a prediction, an out-of-scope line and a live proof (foundation/specgate.py) reads 0.444 (n = None; source: foundation/specgate.py over docs/issues). Share of essential variables (platform and tenant) whose latest reading in the last 7 days has a value (ops/ultrastability.jsonl) reads 0.717 (n = 46; source: ops/ultrastability.jsonl, latest reading per variable in the last 7 days). Share of settled actions (decisions, growth experiments, second-loop steps) that carry an efficiency verdict as well as an effectiveness verdict (foundation/freeadapt.py) reads 0.874 (n = 199; source: ops/decisions/outcomes.jsonl, ops/growth/experiments.json and ops/ultrastability.jsonl). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- Reading. The whole working paper was read from the IESE PDF the owner supplied; the passages quoted in the findings are verbatim.
- Members. Pérez López's members are people with motives. The members whose acceptance is read here are the executor's attempts on work orders (merged against discarded); a model has no motives, so attractiveness is an operational analogue of his concept, not a claim about motivation.
- Attribution. An essential variable that left its limits while an action was open is counted against every action open at the time. Co-occurrence is not causation, so the count of incomplete-model actions is an upper bound on the actions that really caused a disturbance.
- Effectiveness of an action is the verdict its own loop recorded (a decision scored as a hit, a growth experiment kept, a second-loop step kept). Actions that recorded no verdict are not counted, and an action with no earlier reading of any other variable has no efficiency verdict.
- Organizational effectiveness reads k from the latest criticality tick, which counts deploys driven from outside the system; k_self, the system's own share, is reported beside it and is not what the level is judged on.
- Pérez López leaves measurement aside on purpose (chapter IV). The floors used here (half of recent actions efficient, half of attempts merged) are this system's choices, stated in foundation/freeadapt.py, not figures from the paper.
- Source. Working paper, version WP No 5, July 1974.
